sources.title: Crushsound Farmer's Mill | Effects Database
sources.excerpt: Published on April 4, 2012 Crushsound distortion/fuzz/overdrive modulation pedal Information The Crushsound Farmer's Mill is a handmade analog guitar effects pedal developed to produce controlled "broken sound" textures by introducing irregular signal degradation, interruption, and instability. Released in 2012 as an original design, it was conceived as a device that replicates the sonic characteristics of malfunctioning or damaged equipment, such as a failing cable or unstable amplifier behavior, while allowing the user to regulate the outcome. It functions as a stompbox with a footswitch that activates the effect during engagement, at which point the input signal is subjected to crushing, stuttering, and fragmentation processes referred to as "The Mill." The pedal combines multiple forms of signal alteration, including distortion-like saturation, bit reduction characteristics, and non-periodic modulation, resulting in a wide range of textures from subtle lo-fi artifacts to heavily disrupted output. Its circuit is designed to preserve the underlying tone of the instrument, allowing the processed signal to be layered with the dry signal rather than replacing it. The rate of signal disruption is adjustable but does not follow conventional tempo-based divisions, producing irregular and non-synchronized fluctuations. Operation centers on three controls and a four-stage mode selector integrated into the Mill control. The Mix control adjusts the proportion of processed signal, ranging from light surface noise resembling worn media to fully degraded output. The Rate control governs the speed of signal breaking, from slower interruptions to faster, more aggressive fragmentation. The Mill control selects between four distinct types of signal processing behavior, progressing from more stable and predictable responses to increasingly chaotic and less repeatable outcomes, with the final position producing an undefined state of maximum instability. The effect is active only while the footswitch is pressed, enabling momentary application of the processing. The concept originated with Jedrzej Lewandowski, who applied the idea of controlled demolition from architectural practice to sound processing. The electronic circuit was developed by Slawomir Badowski, while Lukasz Badowski contributed to the formation of Crushsound and the realization of the product. The pedal is constructed as a heavy-duty unit with a steel enclosure, powder-coated finish, and true bypass switching. Visual design and physical construction were developed with attention to balancing appearance and functional layout, including custom oxidized screws and a distinctive industrial finish. Controls Footswitch: Engages the effect while pressed; the signal is actively processed only during engagement Mix: Adjusts the level of processed signal blended with the dry signal Rate: Controls the speed and density of signal interruption and degradation Mill: Selects one of four modes of signal behavior, from controlled to increasingly chaotic Connections Input: 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) instrument input jack Output: 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) output jack DC Input: 9 V power supply input Technical Specifications Power Supply: 9 V DC, 100 mA Battery Operation: 9 V internal battery (active only when input jack is connected) Bypass Type: True bypass Enclosure Material: 1 mm steel Dimensions: 180 mm (7.1 inch) length, 150 mm (5.9 inch) width, 30 to 50 mm (1.2 to 2 inch) height Finish: Powder-coated cream white with black serigraphy; top screws oxidized in industrial oil Highlights Analog guitar effects pedal focused on controlled signal degradation and "broken sound" behavior Momentary footswitch operation for dynamic, performance-based activation Mix control enables blending of dry tone with degraded signal while maintaining tonal transparency Rate control provides non-synchronized, irregular signal interruption Four-position Mill control ranging from stable to fully chaotic processing True bypass switching and heavy-duty steel enclosure construction Video all | by manufacturer | not by manufacturer Date ▼▲ Maker ▼▲ Video ▼▲ Time ▼▲ 2013-10-02 Crushsound Crushsound - Farmer's Mill & Ceramic Slides - Commercial 2014 1:18 2013-10-02 Crushsound Crushsound - Farmer's Mill & Ceramic Slides - Commercial 2014 1:18 2013-08-24 Crushsound Crushsound | Farmer's Mill | Teaser | Low Range 0:27 2013-06-29 Crushsound Farmer's Mill 2013 teaser clip! sources.h1: Review: The Farmer's Mill from Crushsound
sources.excerpt: By Paul Ridden November 12, 2013 Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Flipboard Email / Review: The Farmer's Mill from Crushsound The Farmer's Mill Electric Mud Grinder from Crushsound View 14 Images 1 / 14 The Farmer's Mill is now available in orange as well as white 2 / 14 The stomp's moniker is a play on Miller's Farm , the flip-side of ZZ Top's 1969 single Salt Lick 3 / 14 The footswitch sits in the center of a clipped windmill graphic 4 / 14 The Farmer's Mill aims to destroy, mash or otherwise damage a guitar's signal 5 / 14 Three chicken-head knobs are lined up vertically to the left – one for Mix, another for Rate, and the last for Mill 6 / 14 Positioning the stomp early in the signal chain allows you to flavor the effect with what comes after, and lessens its overall influence on the output 7 / 14 The Farmer's Mill Electric Mud Grinder from Crushsound 8 / 14 The first of the LEDs to the left of the TNT dial flashes to show the effect of the Mill, the middle light simply indicates system readiness, and the remaining LED comes on when the TNT dial is turned on 9 / 14 The battery compartment is positioned to the left of a triangular circuit board inside the stomp's 1.5 mm thick steel housing 10 / 14 I found the knobs and dials offered pretty decent control over the Mill's influence on the broken tones coming through the amp 11 / 14 A three-position chicken-head switch sits in the middle, which allows players to completely remove the pedal from the signal chain or select either Full or Low Range modes 12 / 14 Each unit sports a numbered hologram sticker 13 / 14 The Farmer's Mill looks like it can take a good deal of on-the-road abuse and still kick out the jams 14 / 14 The original Farmer's Mill (left) next to the bigger and better second gen model View gallery - 14 images Inspired by the kind of brown or muddy tones produced by ZZ Top's Billy Gibbons on tracks like Loaded from the 1996 album Rhythmeen, Jedrzej Lewandowski of Poland's Le 2 Workshop architects created the Farmer's Mill, which was unleashed, appropriately enough perhaps, on April 1 2012. The second generation has now been released. It's a little bigger than its predecessor, a lot better, and is now available in orange as well as white. Gizmag has spent the last few weeks making guitars wheeze, cough and splutter like they've been smoking 40-a-day since birth, and walks way mighty impressed with the destructive capabilities of the Mark II Electric Mud Grinder. Ever since I watched (and listened to) Jimi Hendrix burn, bash and smash his guitar during his memorable finale at the Monterey Pop Festival, I've been intrigued by the creation of unique tones from the ashes of destruction. Crappy cables, dodgy amps, ancient stomps and faulty pickup switches have all helped to a degree, but success in recreating that glorious overdriven crackle and hum have all been fleeting, and usually ended in the abrupt death of one or more of said ingredients. Last year, the twisted minds at Crushsound reached the end of a long voyage of chaotic discovery with the release of the Farmer's Mill guitar signal destroyer. Lewandowski and company have been noisily tweaking, refining and improving the design ever since, while also looking for a way to bring the stomp to market at a significant lower price point than the hefty original street price of around US$360. "I had a vision of making it more affordable and functional while less predictable," the mastermind and driving force behind the pedal's creation tells Gizmag. "Thus I spent a lot of time working on the whole True Random Technology thing and many more improvements. I used to pay many different people for the prototypes, and some of them even decided to rip the whole idea. All of this put together resulted in this fine Farmer's Mill, which reproduces all the sounds I've had in mind since the early years with the guitar. The most important thing about the upgrade is that it's very musical and offers 10 times more than it used to." The original Farmer's Mill (left) next to the bigger and better second gen model "The earlier edition turned out to be limited in terms of chaos and lacking in functionality (only momentary switching; Mill knob was a four position switch, now it's all analog and tweakable; electric polarity was reversed, now it's using a more popular power source; also it's production ready, we can make any amount of these)," he adds. "I rather think of it as the new standard, the original idea came from me/Crushsound and the plan is to make it the best possible. " The refreshingly analog second generation stomp comes in at just €99 (about $130), although the price of admission is set to increase a little in 2014. In the box At the moment, every purchase comes with a free Crushsound ceramic guitar slide. "We plan to have a printed manual in the future, but for now we didn't want to add more additional costs for the customer," explains Lewandowski. "You simply get what you pay for – a heavy duty and high quality guitar pedal." I found the knobs and dials offered pretty decent control over the Mill's influence on the broken tones coming through the amp The first thing I noticed when lifting the 1.156 kg (2.5 lb), 18 x 15.5 x 3 - 5 cm (7 x 6.1 x 1.2 - 2 in) Farmer's Mill from its cardboard box was the solid construction and attention to detail. From the 1.5 mm thick steel housing to the delightfully smooth action of the chicken-head knobs, it's evident that this stomp is the pride and joy of its creators. It also looks like it can take a good deal of on-the-road abuse and still kick out the jams. The Farmer's Mill (its moniker a play on Miller's Farm , the flip-side of ZZ Top's 1969 single Salt Lick ) has been set a simple enough task – to destroy, mash or otherwise damage a guitar's signal.
